items.name: Pomodoro Technique
clues: It turns a mountain of work into small pieces, with breaks you’re actually allowed to enjoy.
Students, freelancers and professional procrastinators.
An Italian university student came up with it in the late 1980s.
Work for 25 minutes, take a five-minute break, and after four rounds take a longer one.
It’s named after the kitchen timer he used, which was shaped like a red fruit.
Italian for “tomato”, plus “technique”.

items.name: Wikipedia
clues: It answers almost any question, and your teachers told you never to cite it.
Pretty much everyone. It’s one of the most visited websites in the world.
Two Americans launched it in January 2001.
Anyone can edit it. It’s run by a non-profit and funded by donations, which explains the banner asking you for money.
The English version has more than six million articles.
The first half is a Hawaiian word meaning “quick”, and the second half comes from “encyclopedia”.

items.name: Stabilo Boss
clues: It makes the important bits impossible to miss. For some students, everything is important.
Students the night before an exam, and anyone reading a contract.
It was designed in 1971 by a company whose pencils were first made in Nuremberg.
Bright fluorescent ink, a broad tip and a flat, squat body.
Its shape was an accident: the designer hit his desk in frustration and flattened a clay model.
A German highlighter whose name ends with the English word for the person in charge.

items.name: Post-it Note
clues: It helps you remember things, and makes any wall look like a detective’s evidence board.
Students revising, office workers, and anyone running a brainstorming workshop.
In 1968, a scientist at an American company tried to make a super-strong glue and made a very weak one instead.
It sticks, peels off and sticks again without leaving a mark.
A colleague first used the glue to keep a bookmark in his church hymn book. The classic colour came from scrap paper in the lab next door.
3M’s little yellow sticky notes.

items.name: Duolingo
clues: It teaches you a little every day, and makes you feel terrible if you skip a day.
Millions of people learning languages on the bus, in bed and in places we won’t mention.
It was founded in Pittsburgh by a Guatemalan computer scientist who also helped invent CAPTCHA, the “I’m not a robot” test.
Streaks, points, leagues and leaderboards turn every lesson into a game.
In February 2025, the company announced that its mascot had died, apparently hit by a Cybertruck. He came back.
Its name combines “two” and “language”, and its mascot is a green owl called Duo.

items.name: Biro
clues: It writes almost anywhere, it rarely smudges, and you have lost at least twenty of them.
Everyone, including the Royal Air Force, which bought them for aircrews because they worked at high altitude.
A Hungarian journalist patented it in 1938 after noticing how quickly newspaper ink dried.
A tiny ball in the tip rolls ink onto the paper.
In Argentina, where its inventor moved, Inventors’ Day is held on his birthday, 29 September.
In Britain, people call it by its inventor’s surname. In German, it’s a Kugelschreiber.
